rv.q: This is full-bodied theatre, rich with invention, intriguing themes and visual sumptuousness.
Bacchae is messy, loud, uneven; it's also joyous and big-hearted: a whirling celebration of this ancient, yet still vividly engaged, art form.
Whatever the reaction, this production is a startling kick-off to Rubasingham’s new regime.
Some may develop an allergy to Taleghani’s loosely rhyming, militantly unstuffy language and fourth-wall-breaking familiarity.

However these modern credentials come to feel needlessly overegged as the narrative unfolds and Dionysus himself (Ukweli Roach), bouncing with Tigger-like energy in a sparkly gold suit and breastplate, vows to wreak revenge on his cousin Pentheus.
It’s not a staggering start for Rubasingham, but it has got the whole ‘ta da here I am’ thing out of her system in pretty diverting fashion.
The result is a production that is exactly the sum of its parts, and those parts are many, and some are good, and some are not.

But just as the Artful Dodger seems like a misplaced reference within Euripidean tragedy, so the script often sounds off-key: unfocused, tonally untextured, its knockabout comedy smothering the emotional core of the play.
If this unfocused piece isn’t quite the impactful opener Rubasingham might have hoped for, it proves her commitment to bold programming nonetheless.
Worse, Greek tragedy becomes mirthless pantomime with truly dismal jokes.
You need to get through a painfully try-hard first hour.
After sitting through this travesty, I suspect it could well be the last.
As opening productions go, this one is a firecracker, full of life and promise.
It’s a hell of a mic drop, and I for one can’t wait to see what else Rubasingham has in store.
This exciting production is fuelled by a bold theatricality, driven by DJ Wolde’s score and Kate Prince’s bold choreography.
Rubasingham's obvious confidence in directing on the Olivier stage add up to a celebration of theatre.

Bacchae arguably doesn’t live up to that accolade with its messy and issues-laden contemporary approach to Euripides’ Greek drama, but with all the power of the National Theatre’s staging team behind it, it is really meaningful that Taleghani’s play is there at all.
Tragedy requires sharp focus. Satire requires wit. Taleghani and Rubasingham proffer neither.
Clunky and neither funny nor moving, Rubasingham’s production of Taleghani’s play is a tedious misfire.

Entering the auditorium, Robert Jones’ set is an arresting sight. A circular lighting rig hangs vertically over stacked marble slabs, as if we might ascend and pass through to this world of brutality and horrors.

However, like some of its characters, the production ‘goes too far’ at times, the excitement and energy of the piece obscuring the plot, protagonist, politics and exposition. Bacchae follows the titular group of women liberated by the Greek god of wine and frenzy, Dionysos (Ukweili Roach of the Almeida’s Cat on a Hot Tin Roof).

The tension is swiftly diffused by Vida (Clare Perkins), who steps forward and mocks the pair for their dramatics. She sets the tone for the rest of the show, one that’s self-referential, lighthearted and somewhat underwhelming. In terms of staging, this is a stunning production.

Picture: Marc Brenner Bacchae continues at the Olivier, National Theatre, London until 1 November 2025.
